title: Mac Bangs Dennis' Mom

jokes.text: Mac arrives at Mrs. Reynolds' door to pick up Frank's toupee
jokes.setup: Mac knocks on the door of his friend's recently-divorced mother with an unusual errand
jokes.punchline: He's there to retrieve Frank's toupee — a bizarre, undignified object that immediately undercuts any seriousness about the divorce
jokes.explanation: The cold open establishes absurdity immediately — the reason Mac is at this door is a toupee. It's a funny premise on its face and sets up multiple jokes to follow. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Barbara: 'You own his hair?' / Mrs. Reynolds: 'All right, fine. It's mine. I was gonna throw it away anyway.'
jokes.setup: Mac questions whether Mrs. Reynolds really owns Frank's hairpiece
jokes.punchline: She doubles down — yes, she owns it, and was going to discard it — a petty, bitter divorce detail played completely straight
jokes.explanation: Barbara's total ownership over Frank's most embarrassing accessory is a great character beat. The pettiness reads as authentically Sunny — the specific detail of 'I was gonna throw it away anyway' makes it land harder than a generic insult.

jokes.text: Mac's 'Oh, shit.' — a single reaction beat after leaving, implying he registered the sexual tension too late
jokes.setup: Mac has just had a charged interaction with Mrs. Reynolds
jokes.punchline: His delayed 'Oh, shit' — 35 seconds after leaving — reveals the dawning realization. The gap in time is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Two words, maximum economy, delayed by a full 35 seconds of presumably loaded silence. The structure is excellent — the gap between leaving and the realization is the comedic timing mechanism. This is a well-executed reaction beat that trusts the audience completely.

jokes.text: Frank admiring his toupee: 'Wait till you see the hair. This is really authentic-looking hair. It looks good.'
jokes.setup: Frank is prepping for a date and is excited about his hairpiece
jokes.punchline: Frank's genuine pride in something that is objectively embarrassing — a toupee he is enthusiastically endorsing as 'authentic-looking' — is the joke. The audience knows a toupee is never authentic-looking.
jokes.explanation: Frank's self-delusion is a consistent Sunny comedy engine. 'Authentic-looking' is a good word choice that reveals his self-deception. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Frank describes his high school girlfriend: 'Wild sex. Whoa! I mean... You name it, we did it.'
jokes.setup: Frank is reminiscing fondly about an old flame to the guys
jokes.punchline: He blurts 'Wild sex' unprompted before catching himself — the blurt followed by the embarrassed correction is funnier than if he'd just said it plainly
jokes.explanation: The 'Whoa!' self-interruption is well-timed and character-consistent — Frank both wants to brag and knows he shouldn't. The beat works because it's specific behavior, not just an old-man-talks-about-sex joke.

jokes.text: 'Why? Why would a person wipe their own shit onto a wall?'
jokes.setup: Dennis and Dee are stuck doing maintenance at the bar and have discovered something horrific in the bathroom stall
jokes.punchline: Dennis's existential, philosophical framing of an objectively disgusting act — 'Why would a person...' — treats bathroom vandalism as a deep moral question
jokes.explanation: Classic Sunny — the specificity and gravity Dennis brings to the question makes it funny. 'Wipe their own shit onto a wall' is very specific and very wrong, and his philosophical framing elevates it past a simple gross-out joke.

jokes.text: Mac refuses to clean the toilet stall: 'What? Cleaning toilet? No, that's what Charlie does. I'm not doing Charlie work anymore.'
jokes.setup: Dennis asks Mac why he isn't cleaning the stall
jokes.punchline: Mac's indignant refusal reveals the show's internal hierarchy — 'Charlie work' is an established category of degrading labor that the others try desperately to avoid
jokes.explanation: The concept of 'Charlie work' as a recognized category is a good worldbuilding joke. Mac's pride at not being Charlie-level is both funny and character-consistent.

jokes.text: Dennis reveals his plan: 'Well, let's just say I got a little date tonight... and as soon as Charlie sees who it is... no more Charlie work for me.'
jokes.setup: Dennis claims he has a plan to get out of Charlie work
jokes.punchline: The plan is revealed to be using his date as emotional blackmail — Dennis's willingness to weaponize a romantic evening to avoid menial labor is both monstrous and funny
jokes.explanation: Dennis using sex as leverage to avoid cleaning bathrooms is a perfect encapsulation of his character — charming sociopathy in service of trivial goals. High character integration score because only Dennis would think of this and find it reasonable.

jokes.text: Dee: 'How does that help me?' / Dennis: 'I guess it doesn't, really.' / Dee: 'Mm-mmm. It sure doesn't.'
jokes.setup: Dennis lays out his elaborate plan — which only helps himself
jokes.punchline: He casually acknowledges it does nothing for Dee and offers no apology or alternative, and both he and Dee just sit with this reality
jokes.explanation: The deadpan mutual acknowledgment is very well-executed. Dennis doesn't even pretend to care, and Dee's resigned 'It sure doesn't' is a perfect straight-woman beat. The economy here is excellent — the joke is in what's NOT said (apology, alternative plan, basic empathy).

jokes.text: Dennis shows up to Dee's door and takes her coat to 'have a look at what she's wearing' like a fashion handler before a blind date
jokes.setup: Dennis arrives with something for Dee and seems to be setting up a date for her
jokes.punchline: He inspects her outfit with the authority of a talent agent assessing a client, completely inverting the sibling dynamic — his judgment over her appearance is total and unchallengeable
jokes.explanation: Dennis's evaluative authority over Dee is a consistent comedy engine. The physical bit of taking her coat is a good visual. Functional setup for the makeup beat.

jokes.text: Dennis walks his sister in to say good night to Charlie before their date as if presenting a show pony
jokes.setup: Dennis insists on stopping by to show Dee to Charlie before their date
jokes.punchline: The entire purpose of the 'date' is revealed — Dennis is using Dee as bait to show Charlie something painful enough to give up Charlie work. Dee doesn't yet understand she's the instrument.
jokes.explanation: Good structural comedy — the audience understands the scheme before Dee does. Rewatch bonus because on second viewing the cruelty of using his sister as emotional leverage over Charlie is even clearer.

jokes.text: Charlie building a house of cards in his 'office' while pretending to do 'business stuff' as the new manager
jokes.setup: Charlie has been put in charge of the bar and claims to be doing office work
jokes.punchline: He's building a house of cards. This is his version of management. Dennis charitably calls it 'a nice house of cards' before Charlie insists it was 'business stuff.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect Charlie joke. The house of cards as management activity is completely on-brand for a character who is functionally illiterate and barely competent. Dennis's generous 'That's a nice house of cards' followed by Charlie's defensive 'Actually, no, I was doing business stuff' is a tight, well-structured exchange. High character integration because this only works for Charlie.

jokes.text: Dennis's blackmail pitch: 'I'm gonna bang her tonight, probably around 10:30 or so... so all you have to do to stop me is call my cell phone by 10:30 and say, 'Dennis, you don't have to do Charlie work anymore.''
jokes.setup: Dennis pulls Charlie aside to explain his 'plan'
jokes.punchline: The plan is meticulous sexual blackmail delivered with the matter-of-fact precision of a business proposal — the specificity of '10:30 or so' is the comedic cherry on top
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The '10:30 or so' detail is extraordinary — Dennis has scheduled his own moral failing with the casualness of a dinner reservation. The fact that he's doing this to avoid cleaning bathrooms makes it even more depraved. This is Dennis Reynolds as a character fully realized: sociopathic, specific, and weirdly businesslike about genuinely terrible behavior. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: Charlie stares after Dennis leaves and seethes: 'Gonna blackmail me? You gonna blackmail me, Dennis Reynolds?'
jokes.setup: Dennis has just delivered his sexual blackmail ultimatum and left
jokes.punchline: Charlie's affronted repetition of Dennis's full name — 'Dennis Reynolds' — signals he's taking this personally and will retaliate, which is funnier because Charlie's retaliation is always chaotic and disproportionate
jokes.explanation: Charlie using someone's full name as an expression of outrage is a great character-specific verbal tic. The audience knows whatever Charlie plots will be insane — so this functions as both a character beat and anticipatory comedy.

jokes.text: Mac announces his dilemma to Charlie: 'Dennis's mom tried to have sex with me.'
jokes.setup: Mac tells Charlie he has a dilemma he'd normally never share, because everyone else is involved
jokes.punchline: The 'dilemma' is that his friend's recently-divorced mother came on to him — delivered with equal parts guilt and pride
jokes.explanation: Good setup-punchline structure — Mac's solemnity about the 'dilemma' makes the punchline land harder. The acknowledgment that he wants to do it but knows he shouldn't is honest self-awareness that makes Mac briefly sympathetic before he does it anyway.

jokes.text: Charlie's advice: 'An opportunity like this only comes around once in a lifetime. You'd be a fool to let it slip through your fingers.' / Mac: 'Yeah, but it's Dennis and Dee's mom.' / Charlie: 'Well, that means no one will ever, ever find out.' / Mac: 'That doesn't make sense.' / Charlie: 'It doesn't have to make sense.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is advising Mac on whether to sleep with Mrs. Reynolds
jokes.punchline: Charlie's logic collapses completely — 'that means no one will ever find out' makes zero sense — but Charlie doubles down with 'It doesn't have to make sense,' which Mac immediately accepts as valid
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout exchanges. 'It doesn't have to make sense' is both a perfect Charlie line and a meta-comment on how these characters operate. Charlie's confidence in his own faulty logic, and Mac's immediate capitulation to it, is brilliantly observed. This is Sunny at its comedic best — the joke works on multiple levels (absurd logic, character revelation, the horror of watching two idiots encourage each other). Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie's mutual excitement spiral: 'Oh, this is good. Oh, this is good. Oh, oh, oh...' — they celebrate a plan that is clearly going to destroy everything
jokes.setup: Charlie has convinced Mac to sleep with Mrs. Reynolds
jokes.punchline: Both of them celebrate with mounting excitement — the audience knows this is a terrible idea and they are treating it like a lottery win
jokes.explanation: The mutual hype is funny but fairly broad. Gets by on performance energy and dramatic irony rather than clever writing.

jokes.text: Charlie is mid-monologue about plotting when Dee walks in demanding her job back. He pivots instantly: 'And you shall have it. Oh, Dee. It looks like we both need things from each other.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is talking excitedly to himself about his schemes when Dee interrupts
jokes.punchline: Charlie's instant pivot from scheming monologue to Machiavellian negotiator is funny — he treats Dee's interruption as a gift, adopting the language of a corrupt official
jokes.explanation: Charlie's sudden adoption of scheming-mastermind language ('And you shall have it') is incongruous and funny. The sentence is too formal for Charlie, which is exactly why it works. Character integration is high — the gap between Charlie's actual competence and his self-image as a power broker is the joke.

jokes.text: Dee's response to Charlie's negotiation gambit: 'I am not having sex with you, Charlie.'
jokes.setup: Charlie has just told Dee they 'both need things from each other' in a loaded way
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately (and correctly) identifies that Charlie wants sex as his side of the deal — the flat delivery of this assumption as obvious fact is very funny
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy. One line, no hedging, complete confidence. Dee knowing exactly what Charlie wants and stating it as a flat rejection is a great beat — it establishes both his pathetic predictability and her (relative) self-possession. High quotability.

jokes.text: Charlie's clarification: 'No. It's not sex I want from you. It's sex I don't want from Dennis.'
jokes.setup: Dee assumes Charlie wants sex
jokes.punchline: Charlie's correction introduces the idea that he wants Dee to prevent Dennis from having sex (with his date) — the grammatical construction 'It's sex I don't want from Dennis' is both a good punchline and a moment of surprising clarity for Charlie
jokes.explanation: Excellent line construction. The parallel structure of 'It's not sex I want FROM you / It's sex I don't want FROM Dennis' is tight and surprising. The audience gets the joke a beat before Dee does. This kind of compact, well-engineered joke is Sunny writing at its sharper end. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: Frank's date reminiscing: 'That slab was cold, baby.' — referring to a graveyard encounter in their youth
jokes.setup: Frank and Angie are reminiscing about their wild youth, and he brings up 'that night in the graveyard'
jokes.punchline: 'That slab was cold, baby' — implying they had sex on a gravestone, delivered with the nostalgic warmth of a fond memory
jokes.explanation: Five words, perfectly chosen. The warmth and specificity of 'That slab was cold, baby' communicates an entire scene of transgressive youthful sex with zero explanation needed. The 'baby' at the end sells it — Frank is still charmed by the memory. Dark, specific, economical. Near the top tier of this episode.

jokes.text: Frank recalls: 'And remember the time we robbed a motorcycle and ran it into the river?'
jokes.setup: Frank is cataloguing the wild things they used to do together
jokes.punchline: 'Robbed a motorcycle' (not 'stole') and then 'ran it into a river' — both specific details of maximum destruction for no apparent reason, narrated as fond nostalgia
jokes.explanation: 'Robbed' instead of 'stole' implies violence, and destroying the motorcycle rather than keeping it is delightfully senseless. Frank's assumption that Angie is still doing 'shit like that now' is a good setup for the reversal to come.

jokes.text: Angie's reveal: 'Well, I've slowed down quite a bit once I met my husband, Carl.'
jokes.setup: Frank has been building up Angie as a wild woman and asking if she's still getting into trouble
jokes.punchline: She has completely domesticated — the firecracker from the graveyard has become a churchgoing widow who stays home with seven children
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection payoff — Frank's entire fantasy about recapturing his wild youth is dismantled by one sentence. The fact that she's also married (which Frank explicitly said she wasn't) adds another layer.

jokes.text: Frank: 'Oh, you told me you weren't married.' / Angie: 'Oh, I'm not. Carl passed a few years ago.' / 'Oh.' — Frank's flat, deflated 'Oh' as he recalibrates
jokes.setup: Frank challenges the marriage claim as contradicting their earlier flirtation
jokes.punchline: The husband is dead, which should be sad but Frank's 'Oh.' is clearly a recalculation of his options rather than condolence — the word carries maximum comedic weight
jokes.explanation: One syllable doing enormous work. Frank's 'Oh.' in response to the death of Angie's husband is entirely self-interested — the audience understands he's checking whether the obstacle (husband) is gone — and the economy is perfect.

jokes.text: Angie casually drops that Carl had two kids from a previous marriage and they had five of their own: 'Oh, shit.'
jokes.setup: Angie is describing her life with Carl, the picture of domesticity building
jokes.punchline: Frank's 'Oh, shit' upon learning about seven combined children is an escalating horror — each detail worse than the last
jokes.explanation: Good escalation — the 'two from a previous marriage' is bad enough, then 'five of their own' tips Frank over the edge. The raw 'Oh, shit' is appropriately horrified. Works as a quick laugh in an escalating comedic sequence.

jokes.text: Angie (sincerely): 'Isn't having children a blessing?' — Frank's visible bewilderment and disgust
jokes.setup: Angie is waxing warmly about her children being a source of strength
jokes.punchline: Frank's reaction — 'What the hell are you talking about?' — treats the warmest imaginable sentiment as alien and incomprehensible
jokes.explanation: Frank reacting to warmth and sentiment as if it were a personal attack is a great character beat. 'What the hell are you talking about?' in response to 'children are a blessing' perfectly encapsulates Frank's emotional unavailability.

jokes.text: Frank breaks up with his date: 'For starters, you've got kids and shit. And you talk about 'em.'
jokes.setup: Frank announces he's ending the date mid-dinner
jokes.punchline: His reason is not that she has kids — it's that she TALKS about them. The distinction is insane and perfectly Frank.
jokes.explanation: The two-part construction is excellent: 'you've got kids and shit' is bad enough, but 'And you talk about 'em' as the kicker reveals that his objection is to acknowledgment rather than existence. Frank would prefer to date someone with children who pretends they don't exist. The specificity makes it funny and very Frank. Near the episode's best.

jokes.text: Frank: 'I think you're too old for me.' / Angie: 'Frank, I'm two years younger than you.' / Frank: 'That's what I'm talkin' about.'
jokes.setup: Frank tells Angie she's too old for him
jokes.punchline: She points out she's two years YOUNGER — and Frank confirms this is precisely his problem: he wants someone significantly younger, and she's too close in age to him
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The structure is perfect — the audience assumes Frank means she's older, the correction that she's younger should end the conversation, and 'That's what I'm talkin' about' reframes the entire thing as a confession that he only wants much younger women. Three lines, flawless economy, deeply character-specific (only Frank would say this), and it lands with the punch of a well-executed misdirection. The quotability is extremely high — this line works as a standalone clip. Comfortably earns its 8+.

jokes.text: Dennis's date catches him checking his phone: 'Why do you keep checking your cell phone? / 'I've just been... expecting an important phone call.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is on what should be a romantic evening but keeps checking his phone for a call that would stop him from doing something terrible
jokes.punchline: He's monitoring whether someone will prevent him from betraying them — his vague 'important phone call' answer while on a romantic date is both technically true and completely insane
jokes.explanation: Good dramatic irony — the audience knows what the 'important phone call' means, making Dennis's explanation both technically accurate and deeply absurd. The date's completely reasonable confusion about why her companion is waiting to decide whether to betray her is an underplayed comedy beat.

jokes.text: Dennis blurts 'I love you' to a woman he's known for a few hours in order to pressure her into sex before his self-imposed 10:30 deadline
jokes.setup: Dennis's date wants to take things slow; he has a deadline approaching
jokes.punchline: His solution is to declare love — the most romantic statement possible deployed as a tactical instrument to meet an arbitrary sex-schedule he imposed on himself
jokes.explanation: Dennis saying 'I love you' on a first date to hit a sex deadline he invented to blackmail his friend is a great accumulation of awfulness. The joke works because the audience has been tracking all the layers: the blackmail, the deadline, the casual cruelty. The 'I love you' lands as the most cynical use of the phrase possible.

jokes.text: Charlie calls at exactly 10:30 — the blown fuse reveal: 'Looks like we got a blown fuse in here. Better get on that. Blown fuses count as Charlie work.'
jokes.setup: Charlie called in the nick of time to prevent Dennis's betrayal — but his power play isn't over
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately deploys the freed moral leverage as new leverage — the moment Dennis is off the hook, Charlie assigns him Charlie work anyway, via a suspiciously convenient blown fuse
jokes.explanation: Smart structural payoff — Charlie's power move is to call and then immediately reassert dominance anyway. 'Blown fuses count as Charlie work' is a great line because it's both a callback and a new escalation. Charlie turns the resolution of Dennis's scheme into a new form of control. Well-engineered.

jokes.text: Charlie's knowing 'I know something you don't know' in the dark after the lights go out
jokes.setup: The lights are out (blown fuse) and Dennis doesn't know Charlie slept with his mom
jokes.punchline: Charlie's sing-song 'I know something you don't know' is both childish and genuinely menacing given what he knows — the juxtaposition of the childlike delivery and the dark content
jokes.explanation: Charlie's sing-song delivery of a playground taunt while holding information that will blow up multiple relationships is a great character beat. The darkness (literally) and the childish phrase create a tonal contrast that's very Sunny.

jokes.text: Mac's post-coital declaration: 'That was, like, the best sex I've ever had, Mrs. Reynolds. Like something magical happened.'
jokes.setup: Mac has just slept with Dennis's mother
jokes.punchline: His earnest, wonder-filled description of the sex — invoking 'magic' — to a woman who is clearly done with him is simultaneously pathetic and funny
jokes.explanation: Mac's sincerity here is funny — 'like something magical happened' is an absurdly romantic framing for what is clearly a transactional encounter for Mrs. Reynolds. The mismatch between his emotional investment and her total detachment drives the following beats.

jokes.text: Mrs. Reynolds: 'You're not gonna start talking about your feelings and shit, are you?' / (beat) / Mac: 'No. Gay. No.'
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to process the emotional significance of what just happened
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Reynolds shuts it down immediately with 'are you?', and Mac's response — 'No. Gay. No.' — is a spectacular verbal malfunction where he accidentally says 'gay' in his rush to deny emotional vulnerability
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest moments. Mac's 'No. Gay. No.' is a perfect accidental Freudian slip — in trying to deny being emotional (which Mac associates with femininity/gayness), he blurts out 'gay' as if it's the word for the trait he's disavowing. This is extraordinary economy (three words doing multiple jobs) and has enormous character specificity given Mac's long-running closeted sexuality arc across the series. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: "No. Gay. No." — Mac's verbal stumble trying to deny he was about to get emotional
jokes.setup: Barbara asks if Mac is about to talk about his feelings
jokes.punchline: Mac's denial comes out as 'No. Gay. No.' — the word 'gay' inexplicably erupts mid-sentence, suggesting he's so conditioned to deny any sensitivity that 'gay' has become his reflexive insult-disavowal
jokes.explanation: One of the most Mac lines in the whole episode. 'No. Gay. No.' — the insertion of the non-sequitur 'Gay' mid-denial is both a character reveal (Mac's deep insecurity about masculinity) and structurally hilarious. The rhythm of three one-word sentences where the middle one is completely wrong is perfect comedy writing. High quotability.

jokes.text: Mac desperately auditioning for a second date: 'Was the sex bad? I can make adjustments... 'Cause I've had to do that before, and it hasn't been a problem.'
jokes.setup: Mrs. Reynolds is clearly trying to get rid of Mac and he won't leave
jokes.punchline: Mac offers to 'make adjustments' to his sexual performance as if it's a business negotiation — his desperation and inability to read the room is both cringeworthy and very funny
jokes.explanation: 'I can make adjustments' as a response to being rejected post-sex is a terrific Mac line — it frames intimacy as a service with feedback loops. 'I've had to do that before and it hasn't been a problem' implies a history of needing to adjust, which is its own revelation.

jokes.text: Mac negotiating a goodbye kiss: 'If I could just have a kiss goodbye, that would be... really great for me.' / Mrs. Reynolds: 'If I gave you a kiss goodbye, would you let go of the door?'
jokes.setup: Mrs. Reynolds is literally closing the door on Mac
jokes.punchline: Mac is physically holding the door open and negotiating for a kiss as a transactional exit condition — 'that would be really great for me' is hilariously pathetic, and her 'if I gave you a kiss, would you let go?' treats it like a hostage situation
jokes.explanation: 'That would be really great for me' is a wonderfully exposed admission of neediness. Mrs. Reynolds treating the goodbye kiss as a hostage negotiation exit strategy is a perfect dynamic. The scene has escalated Mac's desperation beautifully.

jokes.text: Dennis witnesses Mac kissing his mother goodbye through the window — his horrified reaction
jokes.setup: Dennis walks up to his family home and sees something through the window
jokes.punchline: His friend is kissing his mother. Dennis's visceral horror is the punchline — 'Oh, my God. Oh! Yeah. It's a terrible thing. It's a terrible thing for you to see that.'
jokes.explanation: The reveal lands well — a visual punchline the episode has been building toward. Dennis's horror is proportional (we understand why) and the shot structure (peering through a window) is a classic farce staging. Good payoff moment.

jokes.text: Dennis's escalation pitch to Dee: 'It doesn't un-bang your mom... No, you gotta do something worse... You're gonna have to bang Mac's mom.'
jokes.setup: Dennis and Dee discover Mac banged their mom; Dennis wants revenge
jokes.punchline: 'It doesn't un-bang your mom' is a great coinage, and the logical leap to 'bang Mac's mom' as the solution establishes the episode's escalating revenge structure
jokes.explanation: 'It doesn't un-bang your mom' is a highly quotable, economical, and perfectly logical-within-insane-logic statement. The word 'un-bang' is a great coinage. The pivot to 'bang Mac's mom' as the solution is exactly the kind of escalating awfulness that defines Sunny. High quotability.

jokes.text: Dennis arrives to seduce Mac's mom — she's watching a small television OUTSIDE HER HOUSE
jokes.setup: Dennis shows up at Mac's house to execute his revenge plan
jokes.punchline: Mac's mom is watching a tiny TV outside on her front step — a visual detail that immediately establishes her as an eccentric and deflates Dennis's seduction plan before it begins
jokes.explanation: The visual of an elderly woman watching a small TV outside her house is an effective visual gag that sets up the subsequent scene's humor — she's going to be immune to Dennis's charm because she exists on a different plane entirely. Good economy in establishing character visually.

jokes.text: Mac answers the door and finds Dennis: 'Hi. I'm looking for Mrs. Mac. Is she in?' — only to find Mrs. Mac is enormous and apparently anticipated this
jokes.setup: Dennis has arrived to execute his revenge plan of sleeping with Mac's mom
jokes.punchline: 'I thought I was' — Mac is already there, and Mrs. Mac turns out to be a large, apparently unfazed woman who apparently already knows Dennis
jokes.explanation: The visual reveal of Mrs. Mac — clearly physically imposing and entirely unsurprised by Dennis — is a good setup for the extended cringe sequence to follow. Mac already being there adds an extra layer of awkwardness.

jokes.text: "I thought I was." — Dennis's immediate response to 'You're gonna have to bang Mac's mom'
jokes.setup: Charlie suggests Dennis should sleep with Mac's mom as revenge
jokes.punchline: Dennis says 'I thought I was' — revealing he had already intended to do this, cutting off any moral deliberation before it starts
jokes.explanation: Four words of pure Dennis. He had already planned it. There's no moral struggle, no hesitation, no explanation needed — just 'I thought I was.' Perfect character economy. The gap between Charlie's serious proposal and Dennis's casual confirmation that he already intended this is the joke, and it lands perfectly.

jokes.text: Mac's mom recognizes Dennis immediately and greets him warmly — 'I gained a little weight. / Is that what it is? / Looks good on you.'
jokes.setup: Dennis notes that Mac's mom looks different and she identifies having gained weight
jokes.punchline: 'Is that what it is?' with its slight pause is Dennis's reflexive deflection — not quite confirming the weight gain but not denying it, while saying 'Looks good on you' as a smooth recovery. The underlying joke is Dennis's discomfort at the sight of his intended target.
jokes.explanation: Dennis's reflexive smoothness kicking in despite his obvious discomfort is a solid character beat. The 'is that what it is?' pause is good — it implies the weight gain is obvious while technically not confirming it. Competent but not standout.

jokes.text: Dennis's ham-fisted seduction attempt: 'Probably gets a little lonely though every once in a while... Every once in a while you probably want a man, right? Someone to fulfill your desires.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is trying to seduce Mac's mom using his usual smooth-talker approach
jokes.punchline: His script — clearly designed for a different demographic — sounds insane directed at this woman watching TV outside, and the increasingly direct 'someone to fulfill your desires' is cringeworthy in context
jokes.explanation: Dennis deploying his seduction script verbatim in an inappropriate context is a solid character comedy beat. The escalation from 'gets lonely' to 'fulfill your desires' in quick succession shows Dennis has no gear shift — he goes straight to maximum sleaze.

jokes.text: Mac's mom: 'Not interested.' / Dennis: 'Don't fight it, Mrs. Mac.' / Mrs. Mac: 'Don't find you attractive. I think you're an ugly man.'
jokes.setup: Dennis assumes his charm is irresistible and tells her not to 'fight it'
jokes.punchline: She responds not with resistance but with a flat, sincere assessment that he is ugly — a category of rejection Dennis has clearly never encountered
jokes.explanation: Perfect Dennis-deflation joke. Dennis Reynolds, who has built his entire identity around his appearance and sexual desirability, is told flatly that he is ugly by a woman watching TV on her porch. 'I think you're an ugly man' — delivered with zero hostility, as pure observation — is devastating in a way that anger never could be. The character specificity is extremely high: this joke only works because we know Dennis's ego. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: Dennis's wounded response: 'You think I'm ugly? / 'Yeah.' / 'I'm not ugly. You're ugly.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has been told he is ugly
jokes.punchline: His rebuttal — 'I'm not ugly. You're ugly.' — is the most childish possible comeback, completely abandoning his smooth persona in favor of a playground insult
jokes.explanation: The collapse of Dennis's carefully maintained persona into 'I'm not ugly, you're ugly' is a perfect character beat. His smooth-operator affect completely disintegrates at the one insult he can't handle — a challenge to his looks. The economy is excellent: six words that say everything about Dennis Reynolds. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: Dennis storms off: 'Jesus Christ. What is wrong with you, woman? You're saying that I'm un... You don't find me attractive? And you're... What? Not gonna have sex with me? This is ridiculous. I'm... I'm out of here.'
jokes.setup: Dennis cannot process the rejection
jokes.punchline: His tirade treats her refusal to have sex with him as a logical impossibility — 'This is ridiculous' as if the problem is with her — reveals the full depth of his narcissism
jokes.explanation: Dennis's inability to even complete the word 'unattractive' — 'You're saying that I'm un...' — as if it's physically painful is a great detail. The tirade builds well but slightly overstays its welcome compared to the elegant two-word comeback in joke 46.

jokes.text: Dee watches Dennis's failed seduction attempt and processes it with Mac: 'He did not try to have sex with that woman.' / 'Oh, he did, 'cause he's a dirty, dirty pervert.'
jokes.setup: Dee and Mac are watching Dennis's disastrous attempted seduction of Mac's mom from a distance
jokes.punchline: Mac's summary of Dennis as 'a dirty, dirty pervert' — said with total conviction by the man who just slept with Dennis's mom — is rich dramatic irony
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony here is rich and well-deployed. Mac calling Dennis a 'dirty, dirty pervert' with sincere moral outrage is a perfect hypocrite beat — his own behavior is at minimum equally perverse. The double 'dirty' is a good verbal choice. Strong moment.

jokes.text: Mac's phone call: 'Cat's in the cradle.' / 'Time to move to phase two.' / 'There is no phase two. I'm not doing phase two.'
jokes.setup: Mac is on a conspiratorial phone call using code language
jokes.punchline: 'Cat's in the cradle' as a code phrase for whatever scheme is in progress, and Mac's partner's immediate refusal to do 'phase two,' suggests Mac's plans are elaborate, unagreed-upon, and probably terrible
jokes.explanation: 'Cat's in the cradle' as spy-thriller code for whatever chaos Mac is orchestrating is a good absurdist beat. The collaborator's immediate flat refusal suggests this is a familiar pattern. Good character comedy.

jokes.text: Mac: 'This isn't over until I say it's over!' / then immediately: 'God. Sorry. Okay. Relax, dude.'
jokes.setup: Mac is insisting the scheme continues
jokes.punchline: His dramatic power declaration immediately followed by self-deflation — 'God. Sorry. Okay. Relax, dude.' — reveals the bluster is entirely hollow
jokes.explanation: Mac's self-collapsing authority — dramatic declaration immediately undercut by apologetic retreat — is good character work. The 'Relax, dude' at himself is a funny self-correction.

jokes.text: Mac leaving an increasingly desperate voicemail for Mrs. Reynolds: '...Not answering my calls. I get it. You're busy. You're busy. It's a busy time of the week.'
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to follow up with Mrs. Reynolds after their encounter
jokes.punchline: 'It's a busy time of the week' — an almost absurd attempt to give her a dignified excuse for ignoring him — reveals Mac's total inability to accept that she's not interested
jokes.explanation: The specific phrase 'a busy time of the week' is excellent — not 'time of day' or 'month' — the week-specific framing sounds like Mac is trying to rationalize her silence with maximum dignity. Good cringe work.

jokes.text: Mac's voicemail continues: 'I know that you know that the sex was good, right?' — and then 'Oh, they sound pissed. All right, listen. I'll give you a call back.'
jokes.setup: Mac is in the middle of a needy voicemail when someone knocks at his door
jokes.punchline: He interrupts his own attempted seduction to deal with the door — prioritizing a physical visitor over his desperate message — and signs off with the casual promise 'I'll give you a call back' as if she's the one waiting to hear from him
jokes.explanation: 'I'll give you a call back' — as if she's the one hoping for a call — perfectly inverts the power dynamic Mac is trying to perform. 'I know that you know that the sex was good' is also a funny formulation — the double-remove 'you know that I know that you know' logic is very Mac.

jokes.text: Frank approaches Mac for a wing-man outing: 'Grab your coat. We're goin' for a ride.' / Mac: 'Are you going to kill me?'
jokes.setup: Frank cryptically tells Mac to grab his coat
jokes.punchline: Mac's first instinct is that Frank wants to murder him — which is both a great character beat (Mac fears Frank) and funny in context because Frank actually wants to pick up young women
jokes.explanation: Mac immediately asking if Frank plans to kill him is a great character reveal — it speaks to Frank's reputation that murder is the first inference from 'grab your coat.' Frank's confused 'What? No.' is a perfect non-reaction. Very good economy.

jokes.text: Frank's approach to picking up women at a bar: 'Wanna get down? Huh?' — with accompanying dance move
jokes.setup: Frank approaches women at a club, apparently confident in his method
jokes.punchline: His opening line is 'Wanna get down? Huh?' accompanied by what is apparently a signature dance move — the gap between his confidence and his technique is total
jokes.explanation: 'Wanna get down? Huh?' is a perfect Frank line — confident, transactional, and completely disconnected from how human courtship works. The 'Huh?' at the end implies he's doing a move as he says it. Very high character integration because only Frank would think this works.

jokes.text: Mac confronts Frank about the failed pickup: 'Frank, you have never gotten a chick with that move.' / Frank: 'What are you talkin' about? That's how I got my wife.'
jokes.setup: Mac tells Frank his move has never worked
jokes.punchline: Frank reveals he got his wife (Barbara Reynolds — the woman whose toupee opened the episode) with this move — the revelation that this actually worked once is somehow more horrifying than if it never worked
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Frank's 'Wanna get down? Huh?' successfully landed Barbara Reynolds as a wife is a great callback — it contextualizes the opening scene of Barbara hoarding Frank's toupee as the natural endpoint of this relationship. Good structural payoff.

jokes.text: Mac: 'That move always works with the ladies.' Frank: 'That's how I got my wife.' Mac: 'You have never gotten a chick with that move.'
jokes.setup: They've struck out at the bar
jokes.punchline: Frank insists 'that's how I got my wife' — meaning the move did work once, on Barbara, which explains everything about their marriage and subsequent divorce
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Frank's terrible pickup line is what won Barbara explains both characters retroactively — Barbara was apparently once someone who responded to 'wanna get down?' and Frank has been riding that success for 30 years. It's a good character economy joke.

jokes.text: Mac: 'What other kind of things worked on your wife?' / Frank: 'She likes money.' / Mac: 'So she likes money and dancing.'
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to learn from Frank's (alleged) success with his wife
jokes.punchline: Frank's summary of Barbara's desires — 'she likes money' — reduces a marriage to two data points: money and 'the move.' Mac's earnest 'So she likes money and dancing' treats this as useful information.
jokes.explanation: Mac's earnest synthesis — 'so she likes money and dancing' — as if these are actionable pickup insights is a good deadpan beat. Frank reducing his entire marriage to these two factors is bleakly funny.

jokes.text: Mac's terror of Dennis revealed: Dee knocks, Mac hides, whisper-yells 'Go away.'
jokes.setup: Dee knocks on Mac's door after his attempted seduction by Dennis failed
jokes.punchline: Mac is hiding and refusing to open the door — his paranoia about the consequences of his actions has him cowering in his own home
jokes.explanation: Functional gag — Mac's self-imposed house arrest is a good consequence beat but isn't particularly sophisticated. Gets the job done.

jokes.text: Dee tells Dennis: 'Charlie is making me have sex with him to get out of Charlie work.' / Dennis: 'Am I the only one around here who's not getting laid?'
jokes.setup: Dee reveals Charlie's coercive scheme to Dennis, expecting sympathy
jokes.punchline: Dennis's response is entirely self-focused — not 'that's terrible' but 'am I the only one not getting laid?' — which both ignores Dee's predicament and reveals Dennis's own romantic failure that evening
jokes.explanation: Excellent Dennis line. Dee presents a genuine problem (being coerced into sex) and Dennis's response is to frame it as a scorecard on which he's losing. 'Am I the only one around here who's not getting laid?' is both hilariously self-absorbed and a great callback to all the episode's concurrent sexual misadventures. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: Dennis's escalation: 'Mac's getting laid. You're getting laid. Now even Charlie's getting laid? This makes me look terrible.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is processing the sexual scoreboard of his friend group
jokes.punchline: 'This makes me look terrible' — Dennis's primary concern is his reputation relative to his friends, not any moral dimension of the situation
jokes.explanation: 'This makes me look terrible' as the punchline to a list that includes Charlie (the group's lowest-status member) getting sex is very Dennis. The logic — his social standing is determined by relative sexual activity — is a great character reveal delivered efficiently.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'You ought to do something worse than that... Something much, much worse.'
jokes.setup: Dee wants to confront Charlie about his coercion scheme
jokes.punchline: Dennis adopts the exact same 'something worse' framing he used earlier to suggest revenge sex — it's become a running gag: the solution to any social transgression in this world is escalating sexual revenge
jokes.explanation: The running gag of 'you gotta do something worse' is well-established by this point and the callback works. The repetition is intentional — these characters have one problem-solving template and it always involves sexual escalation.

jokes.text: Dennis shows up at Mrs. Kelly's (his date's mother's?) door with chocolates, trying to seduce yet another elderly woman
jokes.setup: Dennis's revenge plan has spiraled to seducing a third older woman
jokes.punchline: He shows up with chocolates — a classic suitor's gift — wielded in service of petty, transactional revenge. The escalation from 'bang Mac's mom' to now a third mother figure is absurdist in its escalation
jokes.explanation: The escalation of revenge sex targets is absurdist and funny, but slightly loses steam on the third iteration. The chocolate detail is a nice touch — Dennis is performing romance while in revenge mode.

jokes.text: Mrs. Kelly's reaction to learning Dennis slept with 'old people': 'He said he loved me! / How dare he do that? / I'm gonna stab him. / I'm gonna stab his face off.'
jokes.setup: Dee reveals to Mrs. Kelly that Dennis (who claimed to love her) is now hitting on other older women
jokes.punchline: 'I'm gonna stab his face off' — the escalation from hurt to homicidal rage in two beats, with 'stab his face off' as an unusually graphic and specific threat
jokes.explanation: 'Stab his face off' is a weirdly specific and therefore funny threat. The reveal that Dennis's 'I love you' (which he said as a tactical move) landed as sincere is a good callback payoff. Dee's manipulative use of this information to recruit Mrs. Kelly into the revenge chain is appropriately dark.

jokes.text: Dee: 'I'm gonna stab him. I'm gonna stab his face off.'
jokes.setup: Dee is furious at Dennis for sleeping with Mrs. Kelly
jokes.punchline: 'I'm gonna stab his face off' — the specific escalation from stabbing to face-removal as a unit of revenge — is an absurdly specific threat that reveals Dee's anger spiraling
jokes.explanation: 'I'm gonna stab his face off' is a great escalation — not just stabbing, but specifically detaching his face. The specificity is the joke. Good Dee moment in a show that often leaves her as the target of jokes rather than a vehicle for them.

jokes.text: Dee's advice to Mrs. Kelly: 'No. Stabbing's bad. You need to do something worse... Something much, much worse. You gotta sleep with Charlie.'
jokes.setup: Mrs. Kelly wants to stab Dennis; Dee redirects her
jokes.punchline: Dee deploys the 'something much, much worse' formula she learned from Dennis — now the running gag has propagated to a third character — and the resolution is 'sleep with Charlie,' completing the cycle
jokes.explanation: The running gag has now fully propagated — Dee has absorbed the 'something worse' logic and is applying it herself. The solution 'sleep with Charlie' closes the revenge loop while opening a new one. Good structural comedy.

jokes.text: Charlie is rejected by Mrs. Kelly: 'I just don't find you sexually attractive.' / Charlie: 'Are you kidding me? You don't find me sexually attractive?'
jokes.setup: Charlie (who has been sleeping with Dennis's mom and leveraging Dee) is now being rejected by a woman the gang specifically recruited to sleep with him
jokes.punchline: Even a woman recruited specifically to sleep with Charlie won't sleep with Charlie — which retroactively makes all his schemes in this episode both more pathetic and more impressive
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback to the Mrs. Mac / Dennis ugly rejection beat — now Charlie faces the same rejection. The pattern of these men being flatly told they are unattractive is a solid running theme. Charlie's wounded repetition mirrors Dennis's perfectly.

jokes.text: Charlie's meltdown: 'What in the hell is going on? What is wrong with you people? I am sexually a... I am sexually attractive. I am an attractive... man.'
jokes.setup: Charlie has now been rejected by Mrs. Kelly despite being set up with her
jokes.punchline: He can't even complete the sentence 'I am sexually attractive' — the words seem to dissolve under examination — and his final 'I am an attractive... man' trails off in the saddest possible way
jokes.explanation: Excellent parallel to Dennis's meltdown, but Charlie's version is more poignant and funnier because his self-assessment carries even less conviction. 'I am an attractive... man.' — the pause before 'man' as if he's not entirely sure of even that — is a devastating character beat. The trailing-off structure perfectly mirrors Dennis's similar collapse (joke 46) but escalates it. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: Mac reveals the $443 as a phase of his scheme: 'Bam. $443.'
jokes.setup: Mac seems to be in a tense confrontation that might turn violent
jokes.punchline: He pulls out cash — revealing that his 'phase two' involved paying someone off, and $443 is the specific, non-round number he has arrived at
jokes.explanation: $443 as the specific amount is funny — it's clearly not a round bribe number, suggesting Mac did actual calculations or is offering his entire liquid assets. 'Bam.' as a reveal of cash instead of a weapon is a good misdirection beat.

jokes.text: Charlie produces $443 in cash: 'Bam. What the hell is that? $443.'
jokes.setup: It's unclear what the $443 is for — Charlie is apparently using it as leverage
jokes.punchline: The completely random specificity of '$443' — not $400, not $500, but exactly $443 — implies Charlie has been hoarding this exact amount for some specific purpose, which makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: The specific non-round number $443 is classically Charlie — not a convenient round number but an exact, peculiar amount that suggests it's his entire life savings or some carefully preserved sum. The 'Bam' delivery adds to it. This is the kind of specific absurdist detail that elevates Sunny above standard sitcoms.

jokes.text: Mrs. Reynolds tells Mac: 'I only slept with you to piss Frank off. Afterward I felt like I was gonna throw up.' / Mac: 'So Frank makes you want to throw up?' / Mrs. Reynolds: 'No. You're not listening. It's you that makes me want to throw up.'
jokes.setup: Mrs. Reynolds is explaining her motivation for sleeping with Mac
jokes.punchline: Mac tries to deflect the insult onto Frank, and Mrs. Reynolds patiently corrects him: it is specifically Mac who induces nausea
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best exchanges. The structure is impeccable: Mac is told he was just used to spite Frank, and his instinct is to process this as 'Frank = disgusting,' which would salvage some dignity. Mrs. Reynolds' patient correction — 'No. You're not listening. It's YOU that makes me want to throw up' — is delivered with the calm of someone explaining something to a child. The rhythm (you're not listening / It's YOU) is excellent, and the character specificity is high — only Barbara Reynolds, in her post-divorce bitterness and bluntness, delivers this with that particular tone. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: "So Frank makes you want to throw up?" / Barbara: "No. You're not listening. It's you that makes me want to throw up."
jokes.setup: Mac tries to reinterpret Barbara's disgust as being directed at Frank
jokes.punchline: Barbara patiently clarifies: it's Mac specifically who made her nauseous, not Frank
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-beat exchange. Mac's self-protective misread — 'it was about Frank, not me' — is exactly what his ego needs to hear, and Barbara's patient clarification 'No. You're not listening. It's you' is delivered with the calm of someone explaining something simple. The specificity of 'you're not listening' before the correction is excellent.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Oh. So you don't want to be my girlfriend anymore?'
jokes.setup: Mac has just been told he makes Mrs. Reynolds want to vomit and was only used for revenge
jokes.punchline: He processes all of this into 'so you don't want to be my girlfriend anymore?' — implying he thought they were in a relationship, which is both delusional and pathetic
jokes.explanation: Perfect Mac line. After being told he was used for revenge and induces nausea, the entire thing is filtered through 'so we're not dating then?' The word 'anymore' implies Mac believed there was an ongoing relationship — with the woman who refused to give him her number and tried to close the door on him. The gap between Mac's perception and reality is the whole joke, and 'girlfriend' is the precise word that maximizes the gap. Highly quotable. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Oh. So you don't want to be my girlfriend anymore?'
jokes.setup: Barbara has just told Mac she wants to throw up when she thinks of him
jokes.punchline: Mac's takeaway from 'you make me want to throw up' is to wonder if they're still dating — revealing his complete failure to process rejection and his absurd romantic hope
jokes.explanation: Mac's question — 'So you don't want to be my girlfriend anymore?' — after being told he induces nausea is perfectly Mac. It assumes they were ever in a relationship, it uses 'anymore' as if there was an established status, and it treats vomit-inducing revulsion as a minor relationship obstacle. Exceptional character specificity with tremendous economy. One of the best Mac moments in the episode.

jokes.text: Mac catches Dennis attempting to hook up with Mac's mom: the confrontation and Dennis's 'Wait, let me explain'
jokes.setup: Mac arrives to find Dennis at his mother's house
jokes.punchline: Mac's 'Oh, shit!' and Dennis's immediate guilty spin into 'let me explain' — the confrontation that the episode has been building toward — lands with the compressed energy of a farce climax
jokes.explanation: The confrontation is structurally necessary and delivers on the setup but isn't particularly inventive as a joke. Its value is structural — the payoff moment in a well-constructed episode farce. Impact is high due to accumulated context.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Oh, man. That is such a relief.'
jokes.setup: Dennis tells Mac he 'thinks he knows how Mac is feeling' about the situation
jokes.punchline: Mac's 'Oh, man. That is such a relief' — responding to Dennis's false claim of empathy with genuine gratitude — sets up Dennis's incoming 'check this out' (which is clearly not a hug)
jokes.explanation: Mac's relieved trust in Dennis's false empathy is a good beat that sets up an implied physical response (Dennis does something to Mac off-camera). The gap between Mac's relief and what's coming is the joke. Functional transitional comedy.

jokes.text: Charlie's scheme reveal: he set up Dennis's date with a waitress as the prize for his cooperation — 'Your date with the waitress is all set up.'
jokes.setup: Dee asks how Charlie pulled off the scheme, specifically how he knew Mrs. Reynolds wouldn't sleep with Dennis
jokes.punchline: Charlie's response is essentially a shrug — 'Guess I kind of overlooked that detail' — revealing the scheme had an enormous logical gap that worked by accident
jokes.explanation: Charlie's admission that his apparently elaborate scheme had a giant unexamined flaw is excellent character comedy — he's the manager, he has plans, but the plans have holes he doesn't notice. 'Guess I kind of overlooked that detail' as a shrug is perfectly Charlie.

jokes.text: Charlie: 'You've done well. And your date with the waitress is all set up.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is reviewing Dee's work on his behalf
jokes.punchline: Charlie evaluating Dee with 'you've done well' — with the pomposity of a Mafia boss or corporate manager — is an absurd power inversion for a character who normally cleans the toilets
jokes.explanation: Charlie's brief tenure as the most powerful person in the bar, reviewing Dee's performance with 'you've done well,' is a good power inversion payoff. His management voice is funny on its own.

jokes.text: Phase three / phase four negotiation: Charlie announces 'time for phase three, Dee' / Dee: 'No, Charlie, you said there were only two phases.' / Charlie: 'This one's easy.'
jokes.setup: Charlie's scheme has concluded (supposedly) and he announces there's another phase
jokes.punchline: The phases keep multiplying despite Charlie's promises — when Dee refuses phase four, he tries to 'squeak a phase four in'
jokes.explanation: 'Squeak a phase four in' is a great phrase — 'squeak' as a verb for sneaking in an additional scheme phase is very specific and funny. The escalating number of phases reflects Charlie's ad-hoc scheming perfectly.

jokes.text: Charlie immediately reassigns his former Charlie work after being freed from it: 'You guys, can you do me a favor and not get too drunk? 'Cause I got some kegs that need changing. There's some rats down in the rattraps.'
jokes.setup: Charlie has just been released from his managerial power and nominally returned to bartending
jokes.punchline: He immediately assigns the keg-changing and rat-trap duties to others — the work he 'doesn't do anymore' — seamlessly delegating Charlie work to people who don't do Charlie work
jokes.explanation: Good callback that closes the Charlie work arc — the final joke in the C-plot is Charlie trying to permanently escape his designated duties. His transition from manager back to employee is seamless in its corruption.

jokes.text: Charlie immediately after being freed of authority: 'Hey, guys, can you do me a favor and not get too drunk? I got some kegs that need changing. There's some rats down in the rattraps.'
jokes.setup: Charlie has just officially ended his reign as manager and released Dee from Charlie work
jokes.punchline: His VERY NEXT ACTION is to assign kegs and rat traps — i.e., Charlie work — back to himself and others, immediately reverting to his natural role
jokes.explanation: The immediate return to Charlie's normal role — asking people not to get too drunk so he can deal with the mundane horrors of the bar — is a satisfying structural circle. 'You are hereby released of all Charlie work' followed immediately by kegs and rats is a perfect ironic callback.

jokes.text: Barbara's revelation speech: 'I had sex with your dad. / That's right, I had sex with your father because, just like you, I like my sex old and ugly.'
jokes.setup: Barbara has arrived at the bar to confront the group
jokes.punchline: 'I like my sex old and ugly' — Barbara's first post-divorce sexual encounter is with the same pool of aged, unattractive people she claims her children prefer, delivered as an indictment
jokes.explanation: Barbara weaponizing Dennis's sexual behavior as justification for her own is a very strong character moment. 'I like my sex old and ugly' as a phrase is excellent — specific, biting, and self-deprecating in a way that makes it funnier. The delivery as an accusation directed at Dennis is perfectly calibrated.

jokes.text: Barbara on the toupee falling off during sex: 'And with fake hair on their heads that falls off when you're having sex with 'em. It just falls off because that's what you do, Dennis Reynolds.'
jokes.setup: Barbara is cataloguing the indignities of post-divorce life
jokes.punchline: The toupee — the first object in the episode, retrieved by Mac in the cold open — has now fallen off Frank's head during sex with Barbara, completing the most elaborate callback in the episode
jokes.explanation: One of the best structural jokes in the episode. The toupee from the cold open — retrieved, admired, and deployed by Frank for his date — has now fallen off during sex with his ex-wife, completing a perfect circular story. 'It just falls off because that's what you do, Dennis Reynolds' is a great misdirect (why is she addressing Dennis about Frank's sex life?) that works because she's using it as an indictment of the whole family. The callback structure is masterful — the episode planted the toupee in the first 30 seconds and pays it off in the final scene. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: Barbara's logic: 'You said you loved me, so I thought, okay, I love you too. How do you show love? You go and have sex with old people. So that's what I did too!'
jokes.setup: Barbara is explaining why she slept with Frank — she heard Dennis say 'I love you' and interpreted his expression of love as 'having sex with old people'
jokes.punchline: The logic chain — 'love → sex with old people → therefore I slept with your dad' — is insane but delivered with total conviction, making Barbara the logical conclusion of the episode's escalating chain of revenge sex
jokes.explanation: Perfect closing joke. Barbara's reasoning is insane but internally consistent with the episode's logic: in this world, 'love' and 'sex with inappropriate people' are essentially synonymous. Her conclusion — 'that's what I did too!' — lands as both the punchline and the thesis statement of the episode. It's a great structural callback (Dennis's tactical 'I love you' comes back as the cause of his own worst nightmare) and a perfect character moment for Barbara, who is revealed to be as crazy as the rest of them. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: "It just falls off because that's what you do, Dennis Reynolds. You like to have sex with old people."
jokes.setup: Barbara is mid-rant connecting Frank's toupee to Dennis's behavior
jokes.punchline: She assigns Dennis personal responsibility for Frank's toupee falling off during sex — the logic chain is insane but delivered with conviction
jokes.explanation: Barbara's logic is completely unhinged but she delivers it with total authority. 'That's what you do, Dennis Reynolds' as an indictment of his entire character based on something that happened during her sex with Frank is very funny.

tmdb_overview: Barbara hooks up with Mac to make Frank jealous, which leads to retaliation from Dennis.
